title: Is one in five a lot or a little?
hook: One friendship in five crosses groups. Without a yardstick, that number tells you nothing.

doesNotKnow: that the yardstick for 'friends sort by group' is the cross-group share random pairing would give (about 2pq)

misconception: If one in five friendships crosses groups, that is about what you'd expect when one in three people is in the smaller group.
objective: The learner can explain that with 20 and 10 students, random friendships would cross groups about 46% of the time (200 of 435 pairs), so a class where 9 of 45 friendships cross (20%) shows homophily: the gap from the chance yardstick is the evidence.

claims.text: With 20 and 10 students there are 435 possible pairs, and 200 of them (46%) cross groups.
The stage's real class has 45 friendships, 9 of them crossing groups (20%).
claims.source: Lesson rule (brief): a made-up class. Demo.tsx REAL lays out 28 friendships inside the 20, 8 inside the 10 and 9 crossing, placed with mulberry32(7).

claims.text: In a random class each of the 45 friendships is an independent random pair, so on average about 46% cross groups.
claims.source: Lesson rule (Demo.tsx drawClasses: each friendship a uniform pair of the 435, independently); the crossing count is Binomial(45, 200/435), mean 20.69. Builder's seeded run (mulberry32(41), first random class then 1,000 more, the QA path): 1,001 classes averaging 20.88 crossing (46%).

claims.text: If each of 45 friendships crosses groups with chance 46%, 9 or fewer crossing has probability about 1 in 4,000.
claims.source: Exact binomial, builder's node run 2026-10-14: P(X <= 9) for X ~ Binomial(45, 200/435) = 0.000264 (1 in 3,790). Matches the strand manager's edit in company/domains/briefs/probability.statistics.md (0.00026). Seeded run (seed 41, not chosen for its result): none of the first 1,001 random classes had 9 or fewer; the fewest was 11.

claims.text: For large groups with shares 2/3 and 1/3 the chance share of crossing friendships is 2 x 2/3 x 1/3, about 44%.
claims.source: 2pq with p = 2/3, q = 1/3 gives 4/9 = 0.444 (derivation); the 2pq yardstick is from E&K ch. 4 (section unconfirmed).

claims.text: A cross-group share well below the chance share is the evidence that friends sort by group (homophily).
claims.source: E&K ch. 4 homophily test (compare the observed cross-group fraction with 2pq).

recall.question: A club is half red members and half blue. 15% of its friendships are red–blue. Is that evidence that friends stick to their own colour?
options: No: 15% is a normal share for two groups
Yes: random pairing would make about 50% cross
Only if red members have more friends
recall.why: The yardstick is the share of pairs that cross: 2pq = 2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 50%. 15% is far below it, and that gap is the evidence.
